article.overview:
A sample contamination monitoring system measures unwanted material that could reach a sample from the hardware, containers, tools, air and handling environment around it. Its job is to record a contamination history, so that scientists can later separate what came from the sample from what came from its surroundings [3][5]. The catalogue entry names a function rather than one standardised device.

No lunar payload was found in the sources reviewed whose primary purpose was contamination monitoring. The evidence comes from three areas: Apollo-era laboratory witness coupons [1], the witness plates carried on the OSIRIS-REx sample-return spacecraft, which is not a lunar mission [3], and the Opera prototype developed for Mars Sample Return [4]. None of these is a lunar flight instrument.
article.description:
A contamination monitor is usually a surface or device placed where it can collect the same contaminants that could reach a sample. The simplest form is a passive witness: a clean plate, foil or mesh that is exposed to the same environment as the sample and then analysed in a laboratory after return. Active monitors measure contamination during the mission or process. Examples include quartz crystal microbalances (QCMs), which detect mass added to a vibrating quartz crystal, and spacecraft mass spectrometers or pressure gauges.

The OSIRIS-REx team chose passive witness plates as the most cost-effective method and stated that it did not include active monitors such as a spacecraft mass spectrometer, pressure gauge or quartz crystal microbalance, due to cost and complexity concerns [3]. The NASA Artemis curation team distinguishes contamination control, which limits contamination at its source, from contamination knowledge, which records what contamination is present. Contamination knowledge can take the form of witness plates or coupons, in-situ swabbing for biological samples, and characterisation and curation of flight spares [5].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The purpose is to separate sample from contamination. Lunar samples are studied for trace organic compounds, and the same compound classes can enter from spacecraft materials, lubricants, cleaning agents, handling tools and laboratory air. An Apollo-era review listed likely sources, including the lunar-bound rock box and its surface, the collection tools, descent-engine exhaust, lunar module outgassing, spacesuit leakage and the sample processing tools [1]. A monitor helps investigators decide whether a detected compound is credible as a lunar material.

Time-resolved monitoring can also show when a contamination event happened. The Opera abstract describes detecting changes in organic contamination during a measurement period as a way to assess when an event occurs, for example while a specific task is performed during sample processing or hardware assembly [4]. Applications therefore include hardware cleaning, sample containment, curation records and the interpretation of analytical results.
article.operating_principle:
Two principles are used. In passive witness monitoring, a clean surface is exposed for a defined period. Apollo laboratory monitors were clean coupons of woven aluminium alloy (York mesh) or aluminium foil, processed with the lunar-bound tools or placed inside the sample cases. After return, the coupons were solvent-extracted and analysed by gas chromatography and mass spectrometry [1].

In quartz crystal microbalance monitoring, a quartz crystal oscillates at a known frequency. As contaminant mass settles on it, the frequency shifts, and the shift is used to estimate the deposited mass. The Opera prototype uses QCM wafers with a 6 MHz resonant frequency. Its wafers can be analysed after a test by GC-MS or DART-MS to identify the chemistry [4]. A witness plate can only be interpreted if it is protected from the sample itself; otherwise an analyte may be either sample or contamination [3].
article.scientific_importance:
Apollo-era monitoring changed how lunar samples were handled. Monitoring of the rock box and tools showed organic contamination, and the cleaning improvements that followed were credited with reducing it. Simoneit and Flory estimated organic contamination of Apollo 11 samples at about 1 ng/g and of Apollo 12 samples at about 0.1 ng/g [1][7]. A separate estimate by Burlingame reported about 5 ng/g for Apollo 11 samples, as cited in [1]. The spread between these estimates shows how uncertain early organic measurements were.

Current sample-return programmes use the same logic: a monitor is a record that lets later scientists reconstruct the contamination history of a sample [3][5].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for a sample contamination monitoring system. The examples below cover a historical laboratory practice, flight witness plates on a non-lunar sample-return spacecraft, and a ground prototype. None of the sources read publishes mass or dimensions for these examples.

examples.name: Apollo-era witness coupons and solvent analysis
examples.type: Historical laboratory monitoring practice (passive coupons, not a dedicated instrument)
examples.status: Used in Apollo sample handling. Coupons were processed with lunar-bound hardware or placed in sample cases; analysis was laboratory-based after return [1].
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources read.
reported_values: York mesh and aluminium foil monitors measured organic contamination of about 1 µg/cm2 inside the rock boxes; the micro symbol was garbled in the extracted text and should be confirmed [1].
Apollo 12 and 13 flight hardware was reported at 10 to 100 ng/cm2 contamination after rock-box cleaning improvements [1].
Curatorial cleaning of polished planar surfaces could produce 1 to 10 ng/cm2 contamination ranges [1].
Estimated organic contamination of samples: about 1 ng/g for Apollo 11 and 0.1 ng/g for Apollo 12 (Simoneit and Flory, as cited in [1]).
examples.qualification: No qualification data were published for the coupons as an instrument; the values are laboratory measurements of Apollo-era hardware and samples.

examples.name: OSIRIS-REx flight witness plates and proxy plates
examples.type: Flight-based passive witness plates on a non-lunar sample-return mission
examples.status: The 2017 paper describes sapphire and aluminium witness plates as flown on the spacecraft. The in-flight results are not reported in the text read.
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources read.
reported_values: The paper defines a non-volatile residue (NVR) reference level 'A' as 1000 ng/cm2 of contamination, so A/2 is 500 ng/cm2 [3].
Passive plates were chosen as the most cost-effective monitoring method, and active monitors were not included [3].
examples.qualification: The paper describes requirements and design decisions; it does not provide an independent verification of the flight results.

examples.name: Opera prototype (Mars Sample Return organic contamination monitor)
examples.type: Engineering prototype for laboratory and cleanroom use
examples.status: Initial development. The abstract describes preliminary measurements, not flight operation [4].
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources read.
examples.power: Battery-powered; battery life allows 22 continuous hours of data collection [4]. Power draw not reported.
reported_values: Organic contamination sensitivity of about 100 ng/cm2 for the initial prototype; additional development is planned to reach 1 ng/cm2. The 1 ng/cm2 value is a target, not an achieved measurement [4].
A 6 MHz QCM resonant frequency restricts the lower detection limit to around 100 ng/cm2 [4].
Preliminary measurements reportedly distinguish particulate from organic contamination at about the 100 ng/cm2 level [4].
examples.qualification: Cleanroom-compliant packaging is described as a design goal for the prototype. No environmental qualification test results are given in the abstract.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No dimensions were published for any example in the sources read, so no proportional comparison is made. The examples differ in purpose, so their sizes should not be compared directly.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No mass was published for any example. The mass of a future monitor would be set by its substrate, housing and mounting interface, and would need to be stated for a specific design.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Passive witness plates need no power. The Opera prototype is battery-powered, and the abstract states that battery life allows 22 continuous hours of data collection [4]. Its power draw is not reported.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
A monitor must survive the environment of the sample and must not add material to it. Apollo sample cases were sealed in lunar vacuum and kept sealed through Earth return, and the samples were later opened under controlled conditions [1]. Post-Apollo curation was described as minimising particulate, oxygen and water contamination, but no longer specifically addressing organic contamination [1].

Current planning for Artemis notes that lunar polar samples may contain volatiles that are sensitive to temperature, and that metal components must be re-evaluated for reactivity with species such as H2S [5]. No published environmental qualification data were found for any contamination monitor intended for the Moon.
article.limitations: No single monitor can cover the full range of molecular species of interest in a returned sample. The OSIRIS-REx team concluded that controlling every target material was impractical [3]. A passive witness plate integrates contamination over its whole exposure and does not show when a contamination event occurred. The Opera prototype's detection limit (about 100 ng/cm2) is well above its 1 ng/cm2 target [4]. A witness plate exposed to both the sample and the spacecraft cannot separate sample from contamination unless it is shielded [3].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A contamination monitor for sample return travels within the sample chain. It is installed in or near the flight and handling hardware, carried through launch and return, and then analysed in a laboratory. A monitor design that has not been qualified for lunar flight cannot be assumed to be compatible with any lander, rover or spacecraft.
transportation_process: Clean the monitor substrates and place them on or near the sample-handling hardware. Shield them from direct sample contact where needed to keep the contamination record interpretable [3].
Seal the sample containers for lunar and return transit. Apollo lunar-bound cases were sealed in lunar vacuum and kept sealed through Earth return [1].

Handle samples in controlled environments. Apollo samples were handled in pure, dry nitrogen and cleanroom conditions, and only stainless steel, aluminium and Teflon were permitted to touch the samples [2].
Return the witness monitors with the sample chain for laboratory analysis [1][3].
An active monitor, such as the Opera prototype, would also need power, data handling and timestamping. The Opera abstract describes a ground prototype, not a lunar configuration [4].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Passive monitors need no deployment mechanism beyond exposure and later retrieval. Active QCM-type monitors would need a mounting location, power and data handling. No lunar mounting arrangement was specified in the sources read.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo laboratory witness coupons were used in the handling of Apollo samples [1]. The OSIRIS-REx spacecraft carried witness plates on a sample-return mission that is not lunar [3]. The Opera prototype was developed for Mars Sample Return [4]. The Artemis planning abstract describes contamination knowledge options for lunar polar sample return [5].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft has been assessed, because no verified interface evidence was found. A future monitor would need its mass, dimensions, mounting points, power, data interface and environmental requirements compared with a verified vehicle specification before any compatibility claim could be made.

article.historical_significance:
The Apollo programme provides the main historical record of lunar sample contamination monitoring in the sources read. Its organic-contamination monitoring led to cleaning improvements, and the quarantine programme was ended after Apollo 14 [1]. Later curation continued without the same focus on organic contamination [1].

Modern work on sample contamination monitoring has been carried out for sample-return missions other than the Moon: OSIRIS-REx [3] and Mars Sample Return [4]. Artemis curation planning includes contamination knowledge for lunar polar samples [5]. The historical record is therefore one of laboratory monitoring and planning, not a flown lunar monitor.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
No flown lunar sample contamination monitor was identified. The catalogue name describes a function, so the article covers examples that perform that function rather than one standard design.

The Opera results are prototype results. Their current status and whether the instrument is still in use were not established. The OSIRIS-REx paper was read as a design and planning account; its in-flight witness results were not read. The Apollo organic figures are secondary summaries that cite 1970 reports which were not read directly. Two of the cited Apollo values differ (1 ng/g and about 5 ng/g for Apollo 11 samples). Dates for the two NASA conference abstracts were not extracted from the text. Units differ between sample concentration (ng/g) and surface contamination (ng/cm2), and the values should not be compared directly.

Evidence gaps: no published mass, dimensions or power for any example; no lunar environmental qualification data; no lander, rover or spacecraft interface evidence; and no current Artemis witness-plate protocol was found in the sources read.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue ID 264, name 'Sample contamination monitoring system' and category 13 'Sample collection, preservation and return' were confirmed against lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md.
No flown lunar sample contamination monitor was identified. All examples are historical laboratory practice, non-lunar flight hardware, or ground prototypes, and are labelled as such.

Apollo organic-contamination values come from reference 1 (Allen and Allton), which cites 1970 Simoneit and Flory and Burlingame reports. Those reports were not read directly. The Burlingame value (about 5 ng/g) and the Simoneit and Flory value (about 1 ng/g) differ for Apollo 11 samples.
The micro symbol in the 1 µg/cm2 figure from reference 1 was garbled in text extraction; the value should be confirmed against the original abstract.
Dates were not extracted for references 1, 2, 4 and 5; NTRS record numbers are given where available. Reference 3 is an accepted-manuscript date from the arXiv text.
The OSIRIS-REx paper (reference 3) describes flight witness plates; the in-flight results were not read. Its mention of flown plates is from the design paper, not from post-flight analysis.
The Opera status after the abstract is unknown. The abstract describes a prototype under development; no flight or current-use status was verified.
The Artemis reference (reference 5) is a planning abstract. No witness-plate counts, placements or protocols were verified.
No mass, dimensions, power or environmental qualification values are published in the sources read for any example; these are marked 'not publicly specified' rather than estimated.

Image verification: one image (NASA glove box photograph, Ames Lunar Biological Laboratory) was verified by HTTP check and source-page read. A Smithsonian Apollo sample return container image was not verified because the Smithsonian page returned an access verification page. The Apollo LRL and witness-plate figures were not verified as direct image assets.
Lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.
